prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated at optical frequency, giving clocks of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part, B040, for Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The first round did not weaken the scientific case. It sharpened the statement of what is new. A lattice clock is not a better version of an earlier instrument. Katori's magic-wavelength condition resolves the conflict between holding a large ensemble of neutral atoms tightly and leaving the clock transition unperturbed, which is what lets an optical clock combine the stability of many atoms with accuracy once associated with single ions. Ye's group then took the Sr platform to the accuracy and coherence frontier near 1e-18, and independent laboratories reproduce and intercompare clocks at that level. That is demonstrated, not prospective. In answer to the chair's first question, the sentence I would defend is that the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as the tool that counts optical cycles and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single quantum systems, whereas this prize rewards a new operating principle for a clock built on neutral-atom ensembles. I would keep the redefinition of the second out of the citation and let the demonstrated invention carry it. On the credit, I would keep the pair and have the record note Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups. Seven of eight files converge here, but I treat that as a consistency check on the reasoning, not as the reason.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still distinctness. Ye already shared the 2005 prize, and the 2012 prize covered the main competing clock technology, so a sceptical member can read this as a third award in one precision-spectroscopy lineage. I think the answer given above is right, but it is a judgement and not a theorem, and it depends on the citation stating the principle explicitly and not just saying 'atomic clocks'. A second objection is attribution. Two names set aside Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and the groups that built and compared the clocks, and the supplied text does not settle how much of the Sr realisation belongs to Katori and how much of the accuracy record to Ye. A third is that part of the case, the redefinition of the second and relativistic geodesy, is still prospective. I have also been told, and accept, that as an atomic physicist I may find this case more persuasive than members from other fields do, which is why I have kept the objections in full.

responses.point: Danielsson alone prefers B018 for the IceCube diffuse flux, as a new observational channel with a compact two-name credit, and lists B040 as his first alternative while saying that B040 would be the safer choice if the committee wanted maturity.
responses.response: I take the new-channel argument seriously and I do not dispute that the diffuse flux is a real and unexpected discovery. We differ on the credit and on how settled the result is. By his own account the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors are left out, he has not verified who was decisive for the first events, and the origin of the bulk of the flux is open. The lattice clock is a different case, because the performance is reproduced by several laboratories and the credit divides into concept and demonstration. I note that he says he would not object strongly to B040 and that he calls it the safer choice if maturity is the test. I keep B018 as an alternative, not a preference, and I would ask him whether a citation restricted to the diffuse flux, with the precursors named in the record, would change his view of the two-name credit. I think the first-round file leaves open that he could join B040 without giving up his scientific judgement.

responses.point: Kroll supports B040 for Katori and Ye, regards the credit as cleaner than any other shortlisted entry, and discloses a doctoral research stay in John Hall's laboratory while asking the committee to judge whether recusal is warranted.
responses.response: I agree with the pair and with his reading of the roles, Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clocks and Ye for the accuracy frontier. On the disclosure, Hall shares the 2005 prize that bounds the candidate, but the documented tie is a training stay and Kroll names no connection to Katori or Ye, so I do not think it requires recusal from B040. The committee should record it and let him vote. His disclosure is also useful for the distinctness question, since he knows that frequency-comb work from the inside. His own case against names the continuity reading as the main risk, and I would ask him to say whether a citation naming the magic-wavelength neutral-atom ensemble, and not just precision, is enough to settle it for him.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from KPZ (B005) to B040 because the scientific case and the committee evidence coincide, would word the citation around the invention and development without record figures, and lists B004 as an alternative.
responses.response: I agree on keeping record accuracies out of the citation, since a figure of merit is dated by the next paper. The principle is the durable part. Where I would go further is that the citation should still say what was invented, which is why I prefer the magic-wavelength neutral-atom wording to a bare 'invention and development of the optical lattice clock'. A reader who does not know the field could otherwise not tell it from the 2005 or 2012 citations. I understand why he lists B004 as an alternative, but I would not pair it with B040 now. It would need a clearly separate achievement and a credit of at most three names, and the trapped-ion and optical-lattice theory overlaps both the 2012 prize and the experimental ion-trap work credited in B032.

responses.point: Olsson moved from B046 to B040, accepts that the 2005 and 2012 prizes could make an award look duplicative, and asks whether a one-sentence citation can state the distinct principle while resting on the demonstrated invention and not on prospective impact.
responses.response: This is the right test and I think the wording above passes it. The sentence can name the magic-wavelength condition, the neutral-atom ensemble and the optical-frequency interrogation, and it says nothing about the second. I agree that the redefinition belongs in the committee's background reasoning and not in the public text. She also asks whether two names cover Lemonde, Ludlow and the national laboratories. I do not think the evidence supports a third name from the supplied material, because no candidate for it has a clear separable role in the concept or in the accuracy record. I would keep the pair and let the record acknowledge the groups. I also read her field-closeness note on B046 as proper caution, and I apply the same standard to my own sympathy for atomic metrology.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B055) first, regards its scientific distinctness from the 2025 circuit prize as real while treating the problem as timing and portfolio, and says he should recuse from B055 and related superconducting-circuit material.
responses.response: I accept his recusal proposal and I think it is the right call. On the substance, I still think the committee should apply the same standard of distinctness to B055 and B040, and I note that the chair's summary records that five members, himself included on the timing point, find the boundary with 2025 hard to argue. If the distinctness argument for B055 is real, it can be built over later years, and a second circuit prize this soon would need it to be much stronger than the lattice-clock case is against 2005 and 2012. I do not regard his first-round ranking of the clock third as a weakness in his judgement. It is consistent with his statement that the credit is clean.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on control of single quantum systems; this would decide whether the candidate stands.

How the citation should word the lattice idea. I prefer a species-neutral principle with the magic wavelength named, but I cannot show from the supplied text that this avoids every priority dispute about the first strontium realisation.
Whether two names fairly reflect Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups; I find no evidence for a third name, but the supplied material may be incomplete.
Whether Danielsson, who has not yet said he would join B040, would accept it, and whether independent 1e-18 comparisons are enough for him on maturity without the redefinition of the second.
Whether a second distinct part would add anything. I keep B032 as an alternative only; the three-name credit and the overlap with the 2012 prize make it harder than the single part.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1. My documented professional connections are with Ingvar Lindgren's Gothenburg group, Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and collaborators such as Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato. None of the credited names for B040, B032 or B018 appears among them, so I see no specific conflict from the provided profile, and I do not propose to recuse. As an atomic physicist I may be inclined to favour atomic-physics metrology; I have stated the case against B040 in full for that reason. I am content for the committee to record the disclosures of Kroll (Hall connection), Eriksson (B022) and Johansson (B055) and to decide any recusals in the normal way.
